name: Fleur-de-lis abdominoplasty

card.summary: A body-contouring surgery that removes excess abdominal skin with both a vertical and a horizontal excision, used after massive weight loss to tighten the midsection and flatten the waist.
card.note: Major surgery leaving an inverted-T scar; wound-healing complications are documented.

quick.overview:
Fleur-de-lis abdominoplasty is a tummy tuck variant in which surgeons remove skin in two directions, a horizontal band like a standard tummy tuck plus a vertical midline strip, so the lax tissue left after major weight loss is tightened side to side as well as downward. The aim is a flatter, narrower midsection with more defined waist.

The name comes from the shape of the planned excision. Plastic surgery journals describe it as a way to achieve complete tissue readjustment in massive weight loss patients, with the trade-off of a more visible vertical scar and attention to umbilicus reconstruction.
quick.how: It is performed by a plastic surgeon under general anaesthesia, usually after weight has stabilised, sometimes combined with other contouring procedures. Drains, compression garments and a staged recovery are typical; scar maturation takes months.
quick.risks: Reported complications include bleeding, wound separation, infection, fluid collection, umbilical problems and visible scarring; large analyses of abdominoplasty list more complications than many cosmetic operations. Smoking, obesity and diabetes raise risk according to general abdominoplasty references.

lead: Fleur-de-lis abdominoplasty is a form of tummy tuck that combines a horizontal lower-abdominal incision with a vertical midline excision, producing an inverted-T scar pattern.[1][2] It is primarily applied to patients who have lost large amounts of weight, for whom a horizontal-only tuck may not remove enough skin or tighten the waist circumference.[3]

In looksmaxxing's hardmaxxing category it is relevant for ascent after major fat loss: removing hanging skin creates a flatter, more defined torso and trims waist width, which changes how a physique looks in clothing and shirtless. The cost is a longer incision and a vertical scar, and surgeons have worked on camouflaging scars and rebuilding the navel.[1][4]

The published literature is mainly surgeons' review articles and case series. A 1985 article described the technique in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery, and reviews in Clinics in Plastic Surgery cover refinements through 2024.[5][2][6]

chain: Removes excess skin vertically and horizontally
Tightens the abdominal wall and trims waist width
Flatter, more defined midsection after weight loss
angle.text: After massive weight loss, loose skin can hide muscle and fat loss results. The operation removes that skin in two directions so the waist and abdomen present a tighter outline, at the cost of an inverted-T scar.

paras: General abdominoplasty references list several variants, including complete, mini, extended, high lateral tension, floating-umbilicus and circumferential types; circumferential contouring is common after massive weight loss.[7] In the fleur-de-lis approach a vertical excision is added to the usual horizontal one, allowing central tightening that a horizontal-only operation cannot provide.[1]

Poorly visible scars and umbilical complications have historically restricted use of the vertical approach. One 2019 review presents an inner-scar umbilical reconstruction intended to improve results, and a 2022 case report describes survival of the umbilicus on a superiorly based flap.[1][8]
Abdominal contouring is often combined with other operations, such as lipoabdominoplasty-style contouring and breast or body-lift procedures in weight-loss patients.[9]

A 2010 study reported fleur-de-lis abdominoplasty as a safe alternative to traditional abdominoplasty in massive-weight-loss patients.[3] A 2021 letter assessed its safety in that group.[10] A randomized trial examined postoperative pain control with locally infiltrated levobupivacaine in the operation.[11] A 2024 study examined systemic tranexamic acid for reduced blood loss in fleur-de-lis abdominoplasty and apronectomy.[12] A 2024 analysis of 55,956 abdominoplasty patients compared complication risks across types.[13]

Abdominoplasty in general carries seroma, hematoma, infection, delayed wound healing, skin or fat necrosis, scarring and clot risks, with higher risk in smokers and in people with obesity or diabetes.[7] Wound problems at the junction of the two incisions and umbilical complications are discussed specifically for the fleur-de-lis pattern.[1][2]

timeline.event: Fleur-de-lis abdominoplasty described in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery.[5]
Study reports it as a safe alternative for massive weight loss patients.[3]
Inner-scar umbilical reconstruction presented for vertical abdominoplasty.[1]
Clinics in Plastic Surgery review on refinements.[6]
